title: E48 - What Top VCs Actually Think About Legal AI with Keith Rabois, Khosla Ventures
author: Keith Rabois

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Rabois supports the cluster’s claim that technology will undermine labour-based law-firm economics and premium billing for routine associate work. However, he goes materially further than its copilot-oriented framing by arguing that most venture transactions can proceed without lawyers, while retaining counsel mainly for inexperienced founders and unusual deals.
qs: Clients are basically going to say, we're no longer paying $2,000 an hour for your associate to do effectively cutting and pasting, period.
But the reality is, most venture can be done without a lawyer.

st.t: Conditional optimism: User problems outrank AI branding
st.an: The source does not substantively address the cluster’s proposition about useful legal-AI capabilities, user-led adoption, autonomy, verification or market readiness. It withholds endorsement of a speculative AI-linked trading theory and instead states a broad preference for socially beneficial technology businesses, leaving its position on the cluster indeterminate.
qs: I don't know if they followed that strategy or not.
I'm interested in the business of using technology to propel the future and improve society, which is very different than what hedge funds do.

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: The source discusses Spellbook’s contract-search capabilities and adoption incentives for small and solo law firms. It does not address corporate legal departments as AI buyers, selective insourcing, outside-counsel substitution, or the limits of such shifts, so its position on the cluster proposition cannot be determined.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Rabois supports the narrower claim that LLMs are well suited to language- and precedent-intensive legal work, but the source does not address the cluster’s principal propositions about specialist workflow layers, lawyer–engineer collaboration, contextual systems, or verified copilot deployment.
qs: That said, I do think there is a technology, the logic of LLMs being applied to law is pretty obvious.
That makes tons of sense if you think about how LLMs work and how the written language works and how law is predicated on the written language and precedent.

st.t: Vendor value: Concentration forecasts face diverse competition
st.an: The source documents renewed investment and stronger founder talent, but does not address whether specialist vendors will dominate a diverse competitive market or whether current capital inflows will produce durable value and returns. Its qualitative optimism therefore neither clearly supports nor rejects the cluster’s principal proposition.
qs: So earlier this year, I invested in Sandstone, that company is growing at rocket speed, and I'm actively evaluating like several other deals.
Now, I've certainly seen this first hand, like top talent is flocking to legal.

st.t: Contract intelligence: Business coordination exceeds document storage
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central reframing of contract AI around business outcomes and continuous visibility into contractual exposure, rather than document storage or review speed alone. It also aligns with the cluster’s caution that these are product claims and hypothetical use cases, not measured evidence of reduced risk or improved decisions.
qs: We're in the business of providing the fastest, safest commercial agreements in as automated a way as absolutely possible.
And that's extremely valuable, like having this bird's-eye view sort of.

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s view that access to capable AI products or underlying models is not inherently defensible. It highlights replication risk and law firms’ ability to build directly on base models, reinforcing the shift toward overlapping providers and the need for differentiation beyond model access. Its support is limited because the excerpt poses investment questions rather than presenting a developed business-model prescription or conclusion.
qs: The product capability has never been better, but it's also never been easier to replicate these products.
We've already seen litigators building incredibly powerful proprietary systems directly on top of base models like Claude.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports selective, task- and buyer-specific deployment: it presents AI as increasing throughput and contract visibility for in-house teams and smaller practices, while stressing that hourly-billing incentives may impede large-firm adoption. Its claims reinforce work reallocation and pricing pressure, though they are primarily commercial predictions rather than independent evidence about verification, general competence or realised organisational value.
qs: So what Spellbook does is it frees up time for a legal team to use the same size team or even a smaller team perhaps and get more done.
And the incentive of improving their productivity is counter to their business model.

kp.k: Legal AI investment follows founders, not sector allocation
kp.d: Rabois says his investment strategy follows exceptional founders rather than a top-down commitment to legal AI. He sees more top-tier teams entering legal innovation than historically. Separately, he argues that law's reliance on written language and precedent makes it an obvious LLM application and explains its early adoption alongside coding and customer support. These are investor assessments, not findings from an adoption study.
qs: I have no personal interest in investing in a particular domain, but we're in the business of investing in the best founders on the planet.
But I don't have any top-down, you know, organizing principle that says, hey, let's go find some more legal AI.
It's not surprising to me that other than coding and possibly customer support, that law is at the frontier of adoption.

kp.k: AI weakens software integration and workflow moats
kp.d: Rabois argues that changes over the last year or two have made software and integrations easier to create, weakening protections for incumbent software. He anticipates workflows being replicated, performed by agents, or bridged to new systems without retraining millions of users. Nevertheless, he rejects sector-wide pessimism as sufficient investment guidance: an exceptional software company could still produce outsized returns.
qs: First of all, the ease of creating new software, the ease of creating integrations, which were historically a significant moat. Those have all changed in the last year or two.
either recreating workflows is pretty easy, or agents quote unquote are going to perform the workflow instead of humans.
But the outlier position in one good software company could transcend the returns on all of the cynicism in all the other companies.

kp.k: Lawyers can increasingly build instead of buying software
kp.d: Abramowitz reports that a former litigation paralegal reproduced a demonstrated product in nine days and cites Quinn Emanuel's reported development of a litigation platform on Claude. Rabois agrees that leading firms and corporate counsel may realistically code their own systems, while emphasizing that advantages and disadvantages require consideration. The supporting material is anecdotal, not a systematic comparison of internal development and vendor purchasing.
qs: He came back to me nine days later. He shows me he's got that product. He's built it himself.
I think a lot of top law firms and corporate council may code their own. It's a very realistic option.
There are questions you have to think through about doing that, and what advantages you have, and what disadvantages you have.

kp.k: Customer satisfaction offers temporary protection against replacement
kp.d: Responding to Abramowitz's argument that customers do not readily replace products they like, Rabois distinguishes satisfaction from contractual or workflow lock-in. He argues that adoption friction and uncertainty about alternatives protect well-liked products over months or one or two years, but are less reliable over longer horizons. Abramowitz also reports Spellbook founder Scott's claim that the week of Claude Legal's announcement brought its largest number of demos; the transcript supplies no underlying counts.
qs: If you expand the time horizon to years, I think that's less true. But in months, in one or two years, that's probably true.
you're going to discount that by the pain and friction of adoption, some discount about the probability that it's actually that good.
Basically, if your users are locked in, it means they probably don't love the product.

kp.k: Hourly billing undermines large-firm productivity investment incentives
kp.d: Rabois criticizes Harvey and Legora's large-law-firm opportunity, arguing that productivity improvements conflict with hourly billing and may produce fee compression rather than market expansion. He asserts that large American firms bill hourly except for two and estimates total software sold to law firms at a few billion dollars, possibly up to 10 billion. These are his market judgments and rough estimates; the transcript provides no supporting dataset.
qs: American law firms that are that scale, bill by hour except for two.
And the incentive of improving their productivity is counter to their business model.
And even if they were agile enough to adopt to it, then you're still probably looking at fee compression, not market expansion.
Roughly all software sold to law firms, you know, somewhere around maybe a few billion dollars, maybe up to 10 billion.

kp.k: In-house budget pressure aligns with AI productivity gains
kp.d: Explaining his Spellbook investment, Rabois describes commercial contracts and in-house enterprise teams as its main focus. He argues that general counsel face constrained budgets alongside increasing agreements, counterparties and regulatory complexity, making tools that increase output with the same or potentially smaller teams attractive. This is an investor's account of buyer incentives and product benefits, not measured staffing or productivity evidence.
qs: In Spellbook, we've always targeted commercial contracts. And we're mostly focused on in-house enterprise teams.
Their CEOs, their CFOs do not want to spend more money, allocate more money to the legal team. Yet they have more to do than ever before.
So what Spellbook does is it frees up time for a legal team to use the same size team or even a smaller team perhaps and get more done.

kp.k: Commercial agreements expand the opportunity beyond lawyers
kp.d: Rabois frames Spellbook as commercial-agreement infrastructure rather than simply legal AI. He includes sales, business development and customer success personnel in its potential market, estimating that probably a billion and a half people touch a contract each year. His thesis is that faster, safer and more automated contracting reaches a much larger population than lawyers alone; the estimate is not substantiated in the transcript.
qs: But the people who interact with contracts, salespeople, biz dev people, customer success people, huge number of people, probably a billion and a half people on the planet touch a contract every year.
Legal AI is like a category which is misleading.
We're in the business of providing the fastest, safest commercial agreements in as automated a way as absolutely possible.

kp.k: Contract portfolio visibility shifts value beyond drafting efficiency
kp.d: Rabois claims Spellbook improves agreement quality and portfolio visibility, enabling identification of exposure, responses to legal changes and discovery of similar clauses after disputes. He speculates that an average Fortune 500 general counsel does not know aggregate contractual exposure because agreements are too numerous to scrutinize individually. The described value is improved outcomes and oversight, not just lower costs; no accuracy or outcome evaluation accompanies these product claims.
qs: it's mostly about improving outcomes, like less mistakes, less exposure.
I bet you the average general counsel of a Fortune 500 company has no idea how much exposure they have in all their agreements.
How many different deals have we done that have similar, not necessarily exact verbatim clauses because that you could probably do with a regular search maybe.
Spellbook basically improves the quality and the visibility of your legal agreements.

kp.k: Smaller firms have stronger incentives to capture efficiency
kp.d: Abramowitz describes Spellbook reaching small and solo practices that previously did not buy such technology. Rabois argues that smaller firms can translate efficiency into additional clients, personal time or higher retained earnings under a fixed-cost client arrangement, making their economics more receptive to technology than those of large firms. Neither speaker supplies adoption counts or comparative financial evidence.
qs: it diffused to a lot of small and solo law firms who previously just did not buy these products at all

maybe I can take on new clients that are more productive, or maybe I can just go home earlier and hang out with my kids, or maybe I keep more money because I'm more effective, I might have a fixed cost arrangement with a client.
So the economics of mid-market and smaller law firms in the United States are more amenable to improvement through technology than the American Law 100

kp.k: Client resistance could sharply reduce large-firm profits
kp.d: Rabois predicts that clients will refuse high hourly charges for associate work he characterizes as effectively cutting and pasting, and that half of AmLaw 100 profits will disappear. This is an emphatic forecast without a specified timeframe, financial model or supporting sample, rather than evidence of realized profit losses.
qs: Clients are basically going to say, we're no longer paying $2,000 an hour for your associate to do effectively cutting and pasting, period.
And half the profits are going to evaporate of the American Law 100.

kp.k: Repeated venture transactions may need much less legal counsel
kp.d: Rabois argues that seed rounds using safe notes have largely operated without lawyers for 15 plus years and predicts similar treatment for Series A rounds. He says lawyers make little sense for 90 some odd percent of investments on the experienced VC side, while preserving a role for counsel in unusual transactions and for founders unfamiliar with fundraising documents. His argument rests on transaction standardization and repeat experience, not a demonstrated AI replacement study.
qs: People have been doing seed rounds on safe notes, which basically don't require a lawyer for the most part, for like 15 plus years.
Series A's are going to be similar.
I think a founder might want counsel because they don't always understand the document because it may be the first time they raise money or second time or something like that.
But for a typical VC, it makes no sense to have lawyers on 90 some odd percent of all investments.

kp.k: Foundation models threaten vertical applications' long-term investment value
kp.d: Rabois questions whether specialized application companies can maintain an advantage as foundation-model providers improve rapidly. He predicts that many investments from the last three years will disappoint because their terminal value depends on demand three to 30 years ahead, and doubts that many can confidently retain users over 10 years. He is specifically dubious about Harvey while allowing that Legora may have been a good seed investment. He explicitly declines to confirm Abramowitz's suggestion that investors are hedging through secondary sales.
qs: there are real questions about how fast do the general purpose foundation labs improve their product versus what a vertically specific application layer company can do.
I think many of those investments over the last three years are not going to look so hot because the terminal value has to be there over three to 30 years in the future.
I don't know too many vertical application companies where you can easily say in 10 years, people are definitely going to use our product and not OpenAI.
Legora may be a good seed investment, possibly. Harvey, I'm very dubious about the future of,
I don't have a strong feel for whether that's more true or false than ever before.

kp.k: AI competitiveness depends on energy and industrial capacity
kp.d: In the cross-domain policy discussion, Rabois argues that AI leadership underpins future economic and military power and links US competition with China to energy, manufacturing, education and supply-chain independence. He predicts economic opportunities for the Middle East in data centers and AI, conditional on the Islamic Republic being disabled. These are strategic and geopolitical judgments, not evidence about legal-market restructuring.
qs: if they were to outperform us in AI plus energy, we would have a fundamental problem.
military might is predicated on economic might.
we need to win our race with AI because whoever is the best at AI, will have the most proficient modern economy going into the next century.
And it's going to be the future of data centers, AI. Once the Islamic Republic is completely disabled, everything's going to be great in the Middle East.

kp.k: Rabois supports export controls on advanced AI chips
kp.d: Rabois supports advanced-chip export restrictions on national-security grounds and rejects the argument he attributes to Jensen that selling NVIDIA chips discourages Chinese competitors from innovating. He instead argues that China uses American technology to reverse engineer products and build domestic industries. He acknowledges substantial disagreement within and outside the administration and presents his position as one side of a policy debate.
qs: China is a big market. He wants to sell to China. I don't think we should.
Every industry that China has ever cared about, they have leveraged American technology to use that in the short term, to both reverse engineer and give them time to stand up their own industry.
So I do think different people can disagree. Which is a healthy thing.

kp.k: DeepSeek capacity explanation rests on unnamed insider reports
kp.d: Rabois attributes DeepSeek's reported rise and subsequent decline to insufficient chips to support usage, citing unnamed insiders, and interprets this as export-control success. This is a reported causal explanation rather than documented evidence in the transcript. Abramowitz separately proposes a speculative hedge-fund trading explanation involving NVIDIA; Rabois explicitly says he does not know whether that strategy occurred.
qs: My understanding from some pretty good insiders is the reason why it crashed and burned was they didn't have enough chips to support the usage.
And I think that alone is a successful application of American export controls.
I don't know if they followed that strategy or not.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Rabois describes law as a natural frontier for LLM adoption and says stronger founding teams are entering legal technology.
pts.d: At 00:07:52, Keith Rabois attributes the suitability of LLMs for law to its dependence on written language and precedent. He describes his investment approach as following exceptional founders rather than allocating capital to legal AI as a predetermined sector.

pts.k: AI weakens software incumbents' integration and workflow advantages and makes internal development by legal buyers realistic.
pts.d: At 00:10:17, Rabois says software and integrations are easier to build, while agents may perform workflows previously undertaken by humans. At 00:12:43, he extends the build-versus-buy implication to leading law firms and corporate counsel. This is a possibility, not a prediction that all legal buyers will abandon vendors.

pts.k: Rabois predicts that productivity improvements conflict with large firms' hourly economics and will compress fees and profits.
pts.d: At 00:15:27, Rabois argues that selling productivity to large US law firms is less attractive than serving enterprise legal departments because hourly billing creates opposing incentives. At 00:20:57, he predicts that clients will refuse high hourly charges for routine associate work and that half of AmLaw 100 profits will disappear. The magnitude is his forecast, not a reported finding.

pts.k: Rabois claims Spellbook increases in-house capacity and improves commercial-contract quality and visibility.
pts.d: At 00:15:27–00:19:16, Rabois positions Spellbook as commercial-agreement infrastructure rather than simply lawyer-productivity software. He says teams can handle more work without expanding and potentially with fewer people. He also claims portfolio-level visibility into exposure and semantically similar clauses, including when laws change or a dispute reveals a recurring issue. These are claims by a Spellbook investor, not independently measured outcomes.

pts.k: Rabois anticipates less lawyer involvement in routine venture transactions, particularly on the investor side.
pts.d: At 00:22:01, Rabois says most venture investments can already proceed without lawyers on the VC side and expects Series A transactions to become similar to standardized seed rounds. His argument is based on transaction repetition and document standardization; he does not establish that AI caused the existing reduction in legal involvement.

pts.k: Rabois questions vertical AI vendors' long-term durability as foundation models improve.
pts.d: At 00:23:35–00:25:28, Rabois predicts disappointing outcomes for many recent application-layer investments because general-purpose model providers may absorb their value. He expresses particular skepticism about Harvey and qualified openness to Legora as a seed investment. These are investment judgments, not established company outcomes. He explicitly says he does not know whether investors are increasingly selling through secondary markets.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest principally on professional and investment experience, economic reasoning, and uncited estimates.
pts.d: Rabois invokes his former litigation practice and legal contacts as sources of understanding and diligence, while acknowledging that he has not practiced for 25 years. He provides no benchmark, controlled study, financial model, or measured productivity result for his main legal-AI predictions. His estimate of law-firm software spending supports his market-size argument; budget pressure supports his account of in-house demand.

pts.k: Contract-volume examples and standardized financing practices illustrate the argument but are not demonstrated AI performance results.
pts.d: At 00:15:27–00:19:16, Rabois estimates the population interacting with contracts and gives NBA-game and NASA-launch contract counts without identifying sources. His claim about Fortune 500 GCs' limited exposure visibility is explicitly conjectural. At 00:22:01, he cites longstanding SAFE-note use as a precedent for minimizing legal involvement, not as evidence of an AI-specific effect.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Product satisfaction offers near-term protection, while software defensibility is questioned over longer investment horizons.
pts.d: At 00:13:42, Rabois says satisfied customers are unlikely to replace products over months or one to two years because switching imposes friction and uncertainty; this insulation diminishes over longer periods. At 00:23:35, he frames vendor durability over three to 30 years, with a specific ten-year challenge. His broader software skepticism allows for exceptional companies to deliver outstanding returns.

pts.k: The disruption forecasts are conditional and mostly undated; financing substitution retains exceptions.
pts.d: Rabois provides no deadline for the predicted loss of half of AmLaw 100 profits or for Series A standardization. Fee compression depends on productivity improving and clients demanding savings. Internal software development requires weighing advantages and disadvantages. Founders unfamiliar with financing documents may still need counsel, as may unusual investments.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Large firms face margin pressure, while smaller practices can capture productivity gains through capacity, income, or time savings.
pts.d: At 00:20:57, Rabois distinguishes solo, small, and mid-market practices from large hourly-billing firms. Smaller firms may take additional clients, retain more income under fixed arrangements, or shorten working hours. Large firms face client resistance to expensive routine associate work. He does not provide a staffing forecast or quantify associate job losses.

pts.k: Enterprise legal teams and commercial-contract participants are the principal beneficiaries in Rabois's Spellbook thesis.
pts.d: At 00:15:27–00:17:51, Rabois identifies in-house teams and transactional attorneys as direct users whose capacity and outcomes improve. CEOs and CFOs benefit from budget containment. Sales, business-development, and customer-success personnel broaden the potential market beyond lawyers. These are enterprise workflow and cost claims, not claims about closing the civil justice gap.
